key_facts: The Romans built over 400,000 km of roads across their empire — many still follow the same routes as modern roads in Britain.
The Romans brought clean water to towns through aqueducts. Some are still standing more than 2,000 years later.
Roman law forms the basis of legal systems used across Europe today.
Many modern British cities — including London, Bath and York — started as Roman settlements.
Latin, the Roman language, influenced English and modern European languages including French, Spanish and Italian.
Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire in AD 380 and spread across Europe as a result.

slides.title: What is a civilisation?
slides.content: A civilisation is a society with organised laws, systems of government, culture and ways of living together. The Roman civilisation began in the city of Rome in Italy over 2,500 years ago and grew to become one of the most powerful empires the world has ever seen.

slides.title: Where did the Romans come from?
image_prompts: Simple educational map showing Italy with Rome marked and the Roman Empire's extent shown. Clear labels, primary school style, bright colours.
slides.text: Rome began as a small city in central Italy. Over hundreds of years, Roman armies conquered surrounding lands until the empire stretched from Britain in the north-west to Egypt and the Middle East in the south-east.

slides.title: What makes a civilisation advanced?

slides.title: The story of Rome — from city to empire
slides.content: Rome began as a small city state in 753 BC. For centuries it was a republic — governed by elected senators. In 44 BC, Julius Caesar was assassinated and the republic collapsed. Augustus became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC. The empire then grew for nearly 500 years before the western half fell in AD 476.

slides.text: 753 BC — Rome founded. 509 BC — Republic begins. 44 BC — Caesar assassinated. 27 BC — Augustus first emperor. AD 43 — Britain invaded. AD 476 — Western Empire falls.

slides.title: Who had power in Rome?
slides.content: Roman society was organised in a strict hierarchy. At the top was the emperor, who had absolute power. Below him were the patricians — wealthy noble families who controlled the senate. Most Romans were plebeians — free citizens who could vote but had little political power. At the bottom were slaves, who had no rights and were owned as property.

slides.title: Sentence variety — describing Roman life
slides.content: Today we are also practising using a variety of sentence structures. Look at these three sentences about Roman slaves: Simple — Slaves had no rights. Compound — Slaves had no rights and they were owned as property. Complex — Although slaves had no rights, some were educated and worked as doctors or teachers. Now write your own three sentences — one simple, one compound, one complex — about the life of a wealthy Roman patrician.

slides.text: A wealthy Roman's domus was spacious and decorated. A poor Roman's insula was cramped and basic. Both groups lived under the same laws — but experienced Roman civilisation very differently.

slides.title: What did the Romans build?
slides.content: The Romans were exceptional engineers. They built an extensive road network — over 400,000 km — that connected the empire. They constructed aqueducts to carry fresh water into cities. They built public baths, temples, amphitheatres and forums. Many of these structures are still standing today.

slides.title: Roman engineering — built to last
image_prompts: Photograph or illustration of the Pont du Gard Roman aqueduct in France — stone arches over a river. Educational quality.
Photograph of a straight Roman road through the British countryside showing Roman roads still used today.
slides.text: The Pont du Gard aqueduct in France still stands after 2,000 years. Many Roman roads in Britain still follow the same routes today. The Romans built to last.

slides.title: Sentence variety — writing about engineering
slides.content: Let's practise again. Here is the same fact written three ways: Simple — The Romans built roads. Compound — The Romans built roads and these connected every part of the empire. Complex — Because the Romans built roads across Britain, armies could move quickly and trade could flow efficiently. Now you try — write the same fact about Roman aqueducts in three different sentence types.

Model provided: 'Jupiter was a Roman god.' → 'Jupiter, who was the king of the gods, was worshipped across the empire.'

slides.title: What did the Romans believe?
slides.content: The Romans were polytheistic — they worshipped many gods, including Jupiter, Mars and Venus. Each god controlled part of the world. Romans also worshipped their emperors as gods. In AD 380, Emperor Theodosius made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire. Because Rome controlled so much of Europe, Christianity spread rapidly across the continent.

slides.title: Relative clauses — adding detail to our writing
slides.content: Today we are learning to add embedded relative clauses. These add detail inside a sentence. Plain: Roman gods were worshipped in temples. With a relative clause: Roman gods, who each controlled a different part of the world, were worshipped in temples across the empire. Now try: take this plain sentence — 'Christianity became the official religion of Rome.' — and add a relative clause to give more detail.

slides.title: How did Rome govern its empire?
slides.content: Rome was first governed as a republic — with elected officials and a senate. When Augustus became emperor, power became more centralised. The Romans created a complex legal system with written laws that applied across the whole empire. Many of these legal principles — such as the right to a fair trial and being innocent until proven guilty — are still part of our legal system today.

slides.title: Practising clauses — writing about law
slides.content: Let us practise embedded clauses with a writing focus. Plain: Roman law applied to all citizens. With embedded clause: Roman law, which was written down and applied across the whole empire, gave citizens rights that had never existed before. Now write your own sentence about the legal principle 'innocent until proven guilty' — include an embedded clause to add detail.

lessons.lp_task: Roman soldier fact file (training, weapons, daily life, pay) PLUS a cohesion task: write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) about why the Roman army was powerful. Must include at least two of: in addition, furthermore, also, additionally, as a result, however.

slides.title: Why was the Roman army so powerful?
slides.content: The Roman army was one of the most disciplined fighting forces in the ancient world. Soldiers trained constantly and followed strict rules. Legions were divided into smaller units called centuries, each led by a centurion. Roman soldiers were also engineers — they built roads, forts and bridges wherever they went, extending Roman civilisation as they advanced.

slides.title: The Roman legionary
image_prompts: Detailed educational illustration of a Roman legionary in full armour — lorica segmentata, scutum shield, pilum spear, galea helmet — with labels pointing to each item. Clear and informative, Year 5 level.
slides.text: A Roman legionary was heavily armed and well trained. Soldiers wore standardised armour and carried the same weapons — giving every soldier the same advantages in battle.

slides.title: Cohesion connectives — building a paragraph
slides.content: Today we practise joining ideas within a paragraph. Without connectives: The Roman army was disciplined. Soldiers trained every day. They built roads. With connectives: The Roman army was highly disciplined. In addition, soldiers trained every day without exception. Furthermore, they built roads and forts as they advanced, spreading Roman civilisation across the empire. Now try: write 3-4 sentences about the Roman army using 'in addition', 'also' or 'furthermore'.

lessons.lp_task: Roman Britain map (label Londinium, Aquae Sulis, Eboracum, Hadrian's Wall, key roads) PLUS a cohesion paragraph: write 4-5 sentences about what the Romans left behind in Britain, using at least three different cohesion connectives.

slides.title: What did the Romans leave behind in Britain?
slides.content: The Romans occupied Britain from AD 43 to AD 410 — nearly 400 years. In that time they built towns, roads and forts that shaped the country we know today. Londinium (London) became the capital. Aquae Sulis (Bath) was built around natural hot springs. Eboracum (York) was a major military base. Hadrian's Wall stretched 73 miles across the north of England.

slides.title: Hadrian's Wall
image_prompts: Photograph of Hadrian's Wall stretching across the northern English landscape — dramatic scenery, wall clearly visible on a ridge. Educational, high quality, suitable for Year 5.
slides.text: Hadrian's Wall was built from AD 122. It stretched 73 miles from the Solway Firth to the River Tyne. Sections of the wall still stand nearly 1,900 years later — one of the most remarkable Roman legacies in Britain.

slides.title: Cohesion paragraph — Roman Britain
slides.content: Let us build a cohesion paragraph together. Start: The Romans left many lasting features in Britain. In addition… Also… Furthermore… As a result… Let us build this paragraph as a class, each person adding one connected sentence. Remember — each sentence must link to the one before.

slides.title: What cultural legacies did Rome leave?
slides.content: Latin became the common language of the Roman Empire. After Rome fell, it evolved into French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese — and thousands of English words have Latin roots. Roman numerals are still used on clock faces and in film credits. Classical Roman architecture — arches, columns, domes — influenced buildings across Europe and the world for 2,000 years.

slides.title: Roman culture — still here today

Photograph of a neoclassical building with Roman-style columns (e.g. British Museum)

Dictionary page with Latin-root words highlighted
slides.text: Roman culture is visible in everyday life: numerals on clocks, Latin-origin words in English, classical columns on public buildings, Latin month names in our calendar.

slides.title: Note-gathering — using all three features

Furthermore, scientific vocabulary is still mostly Latin today. Notice: relative clause, cohesion connectives, variety of lengths.

slides.title: Pulling it together — what was the Roman impact?
slides.content: Across the last nine lessons we have studied Roman civilisation from many angles: society, engineering, religion, law, the military, daily life, cultural spread and Romans in Britain. Now we bring this together. The Romans left legacies in: law and government, language, architecture and engineering, art and culture. Our challenge is to write a non-chronological report explaining the key legacies.

slides.title: What a non-chronological report looks like
image_prompts: Simple diagram showing the structure of a non-chronological report: Title at top, Introduction paragraph, Subheading + information paragraph, Subheading + information paragraph, Conclusion. Arrows and labels. Clear, educational, primary school style.
slides.text: A non-chronological report has: a title, a brief introduction, one or two information paragraphs (each with a subheading), and a short conclusion. It uses present tense, third person and formal language.

slides.title: What will our report contain?
slides.content: Let us decide together what the sections of our report will be. We know we need: an introduction, 1-2 information paragraphs and a conclusion. Which legacies will we write about in our paragraphs? Look back at your notes from previous lessons. Discuss with your partner: which two aspects of Roman civilisation do you have the most evidence for?

slides.title: Reading and annotating the model text
slides.content: On your learning paper, read the model non-chronological report. Annotate it as directed: circle subheadings, underline topic sentences, highlight connectives, box relative clauses. Then, in the planning section, note which two legacy topics you will write about in your information paragraphs.

Children complete independently using their notes from previous lessons.

slides.title: How do we plan a non-chronological report?
slides.content: A strong plan makes writing much easier. Our report will have five sections: title, introduction, legacy paragraph 1, legacy paragraph 2 and conclusion. For each information paragraph we need: a subheading, a topic sentence that states what the paragraph is about, and at least two pieces of evidence. The conclusion should link back to the key question.

slides.title: Planning our introduction together
slides.content: Let us plan the introduction as a class. The introduction should: tell the reader what the report is about, mention that the Romans had a lasting impact, and name the two legacy areas we will discuss. It should be 2-3 sentences only. Draft one together. Remember: present tense, third person, formal tone.

slides.title: Complete your report plan
slides.content: On your learning paper, complete the full report planning frame. Use your notes from lessons 6-10. For each legacy section: choose a clear subheading, draft your topic sentence, add at least two evidence bullet points. You will use this plan next lesson to begin writing.

quiz.answer: To tell the reader what the report is about and introduce the topic

quiz.answer: Accept any clear topic sentence in third person, present tense

lessons.lp_task: Lined writing paper with report structure cue strip at the top (title, introduction, legacy 1 subheading + paragraph, legacy 2 subheading + paragraph, conclusion). Children write title, introduction and legacy paragraph 1 in this session. Writing checklist at the bottom.

slides.title: Let us write — modelling the introduction
slides.content: Watch as we build the introduction together. Title: Key Legacies of the Roman Civilisation. Introduction: The Roman civilisation, which lasted for nearly 1,000 years, left a lasting impact that can still be seen in modern life today. Roman achievements in law, language and engineering continue to shape the world we live in.  Notice: relative clause, formal tone, present tense, third person.

slides.title: Writing legacy paragraph 1 together
slides.content: Now we write the first legacy paragraph together using the plan from last lesson. Topic sentence first. Then evidence — using at least two cohesion connectives. Then a closing sentence that links back to impact or legacy. Remember to use a variety of sentence types. Let us draft this on the board together before you write your own.

slides.title: Write your introduction and paragraph 1
slides.content: Using your plan and today's models, write your title, introduction and first legacy paragraph. Aim for 2-3 sentences in the introduction and 4-6 sentences in the paragraph. When you finish, tick each item on your writing checklist: topic sentence, embedded clause, cohesion connective, variety of sentence types.

lessons.lp_task: Continuation of writing paper from L12 — legacy paragraph 2 and conclusion. Peer-edit checklist included: partner ticks off topic sentence, embedded clause, connectives, sentence variety, correct tense and person.

slides.title: Modelling legacy paragraph 2 and the conclusion
slides.content: Let us model the second paragraph and the conclusion. Paragraph 2 follows the same structure as paragraph 1 — topic sentence, evidence with connectives, closing sentence. The conclusion should be 1-3 sentences. It links back to the key question: what was the impact of Roman civilisation? It should not introduce new information — it summarises and gives a final judgement.

slides.title: Peer review — checking each other's writing
slides.content: Before you write your paragraph 2, swap your work with a partner. Using the peer-edit checklist, check their introduction and paragraph 1. Look for: clear topic sentence, embedded clause, two connectives, variety of sentences. Give one specific positive comment and one specific suggestion for improvement. Then return the work and continue with your own writing.

slides.title: Write your paragraph 2 and conclusion
slides.content: Write your second legacy paragraph and your conclusion. Use your plan. Aim for 4-6 sentences in the paragraph and 1-3 sentences in the conclusion. When you finish, complete your own self-edit checklist before handing in.

lessons.lp_task: Final editing and publishing — children write or word-process their final version using their draft. Editing checklist: spelling, punctuation, sentence variety, clauses, connectives, tense, person, subheadings. Space for a reflection sentence at the end: 'I am most proud of… because…'

slides.title: The editing process — what to look for
slides.content: Editing is not just checking spelling. It means reading your work as a reader and asking: is this clear? Is this interesting? Does each paragraph have a topic sentence? Have I used a variety of sentence types? Are my connectives doing their job? We will edit our reports today using a structured checklist.

slides.title: Editing together — one paragraph as a class
slides.content: Here is a draft paragraph about Roman law with some deliberate weaknesses. Let us find and fix them together: missing topic sentence, repeated sentence structure, no connectives, no embedded clause. Edit it on the board as a class — then apply what we have learned to your own work.

writing_features.description: Using simple, compound and complex sentences. Avoiding strings of short sentences or over-long ones.
writing_features.model_sentence: The Romans were great builders. They constructed roads, temples and aqueducts across the empire. Because they used concrete and arches, many of their structures still stand today.
Roman law, which applied to all citizens across the empire, forms the basis of many legal systems we still use today.

writing_features.description: Building on ideas within a paragraph using: in addition, furthermore, also, additionally, however, as a result.
writing_features.model_sentence: The Roman military was highly disciplined. In addition, soldiers were trained engineers who built roads and forts. Furthermore, the army's organisation allowed it to conquer vast territories.

writing_features.description: Title, brief introduction, subheadings, 1-2 information paragraphs, short concluding paragraph. Present tense for facts. Third person. Formal tone.
writing_features.model_sentence: Introduction: The Roman civilisation, which lasted for nearly 1,000 years, left a lasting legacy that can still be seen in modern life today.
